title: SYSK Selects: How Human Cannonballs Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2011 episode "How Human Cannonballs Work." The hosts open with banter about Chuck's Kaboom cereal, Hunter S. Thompson's cremated remains being shot from a cannon, and whether they'd want their own bodies fired from one. They trace the history from George Farini's projector (1871) and Lulu, to Rosa Richter (Zazzle) in 1880s and the first modern cannon, then the Zacchini family, John Weiss, and the Smith family. They cover the physics of compressed-air cannons, g-forces, the importance of the net and landing, test dummies, and safety. Accidents discussed include Elvin Bale's 1970s-80s Hong Kong airbag miss, Matt Cranch's 2011 net collapse death, and the Zacchini sister's collision with her brother. They note the DARPA cannon concept for shooting people onto buildings. Listener mail follows about an Adirondacks home with a tunnel that was part of the Underground Railroad.

segments.title: Opening banter: Kaboom cereal and Hunter S. Thompson's cannon
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the Saturday Selects episode. The hosts talk about the Kaboom cereal clown mascot and Hunter S. Thompson's remains being fired from a cannon, and Chuck jokes about wanting his own body shot from one.

segments.title: Fake boom and early history: Farini projector and Lulu
segments.summary: The hosts explain that human cannonball acts use a fake boom and flash rather than gunpowder. They describe George Farini's 1871 projector and Lulu, a man in drag, who was launched about thirty feet and caught on a trapeze.

segments.title: Zazzle and the first spring-and-blast cannon
segments.summary: Rosa Marie Richter, age fourteen and billed as Zazzle, was shot from the first modern-style cannon at P. T. Barnum's urging around 1880. She broke her back within a few performances, and the hosts note it was the first casualty of the act. George Loyal was later shot at the Yankee Robinson Circus and caught by a woman on a trapeze.

segments.title: Physics: compressed air, g-forces, and launch speed
segments.summary: The hosts describe the modern compressed-air cannon with a sled inside a barrel, launch pressures of three to six thousand psi, ranges of about two hundred feet horizontally or vertically, speeds of sixty to seventy mph, and about nine g's at launch and twelve at impact. They note that the body must stay rigid and that g-forces can cause blackout.

segments.title: Planning, nets, and test dummies
segments.summary: Setup requires accounting for wind, body weight, humidity, temperature, and obstacles. Test dummies are fired first to set the trajectory. Landing in the net's proper third is crucial, and many performers use airbags.

segments.title: Circus families: Zacchini, John Weiss, and Smith family
segments.summary: The Zacchini family performed from the 1920s to the 1990s, with five of seven brothers as cannonballs and a sister also performing. Mario Zacchini flew over two Ferris wheels. John Weiss, a former clown, did about five thousand shots. The Smith family includes David Cannonball Smith Jr., who bettered his father's distance of about 100 feet.

segments.title: Human cannonball deaths and the DARPA concept
segments.summary: The hosts note that about thirty of roughly fifty human cannonballs have died, citing historian A. H. Cox. They discuss a DARPA patent idea for shooting responders onto buildings, and joke about the landing risk.

segments.title: Safety accidents: Elvin Bale, Matt Cranch, and the Zacchini collision
segments.summary: Elvin Bale missed his airbags in Hong Kong after a wet test dummy was heavier than expected, leaving him paralyzed. Matt Cranch died in April 2011 when the net collapsed. A Zacchini sister collided midair with a brother during a double-barrel stunt and broke her back.

segments.title: Closing and search tip
segments.summary: The hosts close the cannonball discussion, mention a Daredevil topic, and point listeners to the HowStuffWorks search bar for more on human cannonballs.

segments.title: Listener mail: Underground Railroad tunnel in the Adirondacks
segments.summary: Alison writes about her great-grandfather's home in Johnsburg, New York, which has a haunted organ and a tunnel from the Underground Railroad that runs under the barn to a strawberry patch.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite strawberry recipes by email and sign off.
